summary: FLAME IN FREEFALL is an AI-powered web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion research to support fire-safety decisions for human space exploration. We built a structured knowledge base from the Combustion Science investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, including BASS, Saffire, FLEX, ACME and SAME. Users choose a habitable environment (ISS, lunar base, Mars base or rover) and the dashboard re-ranks the most relevant investigations by atmosphere (oxygen fraction and pressure), gravity, fuel type and fire-safety pillar (prevention, detection, suppression), with transparent, adjustable weights. A predictive model trained on PSI experimental tables estimates flammability behavior with uncertainty and flags out-of-domain inputs. An AI assistant answers questions citing the PSI dataset and its DOI, and declines when evidence is missing. A research-to-technology map exposes knowledge gaps, especially partial gravity, where the minimum oxygen needed for burning may peak near lunar gravity, and turns evidence into recommendations for next-generation fire prevention, detection and suppression for Artemis-era habitats.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Demo video: https://youtu.be/ZGyjrI0L96Q

Team: ANDORA LABS – NASA Space Apps Challenge Riobamba 2026
Source code: https://github.com/jordy-ricardo25/NASA-Space-Apps-Challenge-2026

FLAME IN FREEFALL turns NASA's scattered microgravity combustion data into decisions. It answers three questions from the challenge: Which investigations matter most for a given habitat? What data can support predictive flammability models? Which research should inform next-generation fire-control equipment?

HOW IT WORKS

1. State of the art and ranking: structured fact sheets for the PSI Combustion Science investigations (objective, fuel, O2, pressure, flow, gravity, sensors, key findings, pillar, DOI). A 0–100 relevance score ranks them per environment using visible criteria: atmosphere similarity, fuel similarity, fire-safety pillar, scale, data availability and gravity.

2. Environment selector: choosing ISS, lunar base, Mars base or rover changes the atmosphere, gravity, ranking and warnings shown.

3. Data and prediction: we harmonized units from PSI experimental tables (e.g., FLEX droplet burning-rate constant via the d²-law) and trained simple, interpretable models validated by test group, compared against a baseline and basic physics, with uncertainty and out-of-domain warnings.

4. AI assistant: a retrieval-augmented assistant that cites PSI investigations and DOIs and refuses to answer without evidence.

5. Research-to-technology map: evidence → gap → suggested equipment or design control.

PHYSICS WE CONSIDERED

Without buoyancy there is no natural convection: oxygen arrives by diffusion or ventilation, so airflow is the decisive variable. Materials that pass NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 in 1 g can still burn in low-flow microgravity. Oxygen percentage and oxygen partial pressure are not the same (30% O2 at 10.2 psi ≈ Earth's ppO2). Recent NASA work suggests minimum oxygen for burning may reach its lowest value near lunar gravity, so we do not blindly interpolate between 0 g and 1 g; the dashboard flags this gap.

IMPACT

Supports material selection, cabin-atmosphere choices and fire detection/suppression design for Artemis and future Moon and Mars habitats, and highlights where new experiments (partial gravity, high oxygen) are most needed. On Earth, the same insights apply to cleaner combustion and fire safety in confined spaces.

TOOLS

Frontend: Next.js (React), deployed on Vercel. Backend: Python, FastAPI. Data processing and modeling: Python (pandas, scikit-learn). AI assistant: retrieval-augmented generation over PSI documentation. Data: NASA PSI, NTRS.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a generic chatbot, the habitat itself becomes the interface: pick an environment and the evidence, ranking and warnings adapt. Every claim is traceable to a DOI, and the tool is honest about what the data cannot predict.
